facts.raw_span: a three-week history of a tender, slow-growing left axillary lump
a low-grade fever (37.5–38°C) for one week
hypertension—treated with lacidipine, lisinopril, and hydrochlorothiazide
a laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass performed two years earlier
lost 112 kg (BMI from 64.6 to 28 kg/m2)
smoked 30 cigarettes daily
took vitamin (A, D, E, B complex), calcium, cholecalciferol, and iron supplements
a tender, non-mobile, 3 × 4 cm lymph node in the left axilla

laboratory studies—including a complete blood count, ESR, liver and renal panels, autoantibodies (ANA, RF), complement levels, inflammatory markers, thyroid function, and serologies for a broad spectrum of viral and parasitic pathogens—were all normal or negative
a thoracoabdominal CT scan was unremarkable except for the axillary lymphadenopathy
a biopsy of the axillary node revealed coagulative necrosis with frequent karyorrhexis and a lymphoplasmacytoid infiltrate
an investigation for mycobacteria was negative

concepts.why: The patient presents with a tender, slow-growing left axillary lump and a low-grade fever, which are consistent with cat-scratch disease.
The biopsy of the axillary node revealed coagulative necrosis with frequent karyorrhexis and a lymphoplasmacytoid infiltrate, which are characteristic of Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease.
The patient has a tender, non-mobile lymph node in the left axilla, and the thoracoabdominal CT scan showed axillary lymphadenopathy, which could be indicative of lymphoma.
Although the investigation for mycobacteria was negative, the patient's symptoms and biopsy results could still be consistent with tuberculous lymphadenitis.
The biopsy of the axillary node revealed coagulative necrosis with frequent karyorrhexis and a lymphoplasmacytoid infiltrate, which could be indicative of sarcoidosis.
The patient has a tender, non-mobile lymph node in the left axilla, and the thoracoabdominal CT scan showed axillary lymphadenopathy, which could be indicative of Castleman disease.
The biopsy of the axillary node revealed coagulative necrosis with frequent karyorrhexis and a lymphoplasmacytoid infiltrate, which could be indicative of Kimura disease.
The patient has a tender, non-mobile lymph node in the left axilla, and the thoracoabdominal CT scan showed axillary lymphadenopathy, which could be indicative of Rosai-Dorfman disease.

rationales.F01: The presence of a tender, slow-growing axillary lump is more typical of Cat-scratch disease and Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease.
rationales.F02: Low-grade fever is a non-specific symptom that can be seen in various conditions, including Cat-scratch disease and Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease.
rationales.F08: The presence of a tender, non-mobile lymph node in the axilla is more typical of Cat-scratch disease and Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease.
rationales.F09: The absence of abnormal laboratory results makes it less likely for the patient to have a systemic disease.
rationales.F11: The biopsy results showing coagulative necrosis with frequent karyorrhexis and a lymphoplasmacytoid infiltrate are more typical of Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease.
rationales.F12: The negative investigation for mycobacteria rules out Tuberculous lymphadenitis.

frontier_selector.rationale: Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease best explains the tender lymph node, low-grade fever, and biopsy findings of coagulative necrosis with frequent karyorrhexis and a lymphoplasmacytoid infiltrate, without strong contradictions.
